summary:
SARnik is a radar "pre-purchase inspection" for any plot of land: a free, open-source web map that turns NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data into plain-language answers about the ground.

Click a plot and SARnik shows what radar sees there:
- Is the ground sinking?
- Does it lie in a flood-prone hollow?
- Are new buildings going up nearby, and how much was built each year since 2015?
- Is the greenery around it disappearing?

Who it is for:
- Home buyers and residents: a house is the biggest purchase most families make, yet nobody checks the ground.
- Local governments: one map to plan flood protection and climate adaptation, track where the town is growing, spot new construction early and watch green areas shrink.
- Planners, banks and insurers: an open, testable overview of land risk.

Built for anywhere on Earth: NISAR images the whole globe every 12 days, and most of SARnik runs on global open data (NISAR, Sentinel-1, ALOS, NASA OPERA, MODIS, Landsat-based maps). Local layers such as land parcels and flood maps plug in country by country. Our first deployment covers Poznań, Poland, and its metropolitan area, where we tested every radar signal against independent data.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SARnik ("SAR" + the Polish word for a small tool) is a free, open-source web app for Poznań, Poland, and its metropolitan area. You search an address or click a point; SARnik outlines the cadastral plot (live from the Polish land registry, GUGiK ULDK) and opens a card with a score and a check-up list: each item is marked "fine", "worth checking" or "attention", with the satellite source behind it. Thematic views ("lenses") show the whole region: plot score, construction sites 2026 (SAR), flood risk, ground subsidence, loss of greenery, a 2035 build-up projection, and the NISAR satellite itself (its L-band picture of 2026 and the raw radar passes in an expert view). A timeline shows the area growing from 1975 to 2035. Everything works in English and Polish, on desktop and phone, in light and dark mode.

HOW IT WORKS

  • NISAR L-band (NASA-ISRO): GCOV backscatter (HH/HV) from June to October 2026 shows the radar picture of 2026 and how the surface changed over the summer (rain, harvest and tillage); GUNW interferometric coherence and SME2 soil moisture are map layers.
  • Construction: Sentinel-1 C-band double-bounce brightening between autumn 2025 and autumn 2026 (VV up by at least 3 dB and VV minus VH up by at least 1.5 dB): a new wall and the ground form a corner reflector.
  • Built-up area year by year: 265 radar passes over 12 years (Sentinel-1 every summer 2015–2026, NISAR 2026, ALOS PALSAR 2007–2010). The optical built-up map ends in 2020, so radar is the only source for what was built after it.
  • Ground motion: EGMS InSAR (2016–2020). Flood risk: PIG-PIB groundwater-flood areas plus terrain hollows from the Copernicus DEM (TanDEM-X radar).
  • Greenery and heat: Hansen Global Forest Change (Landsat) and NASA MODIS land surface temperature and vegetation.
  • 2035 projection: a logistic model trained on 2005–2015 and tested on 2015–2020 (Landsat-based GHSL), computed only on land that radar still sees as open.

The data pipeline (Python) downloads and processes the satellite data into small grids; the web app (plain JavaScript and Leaflet) needs no server or database and runs from static files.

WHY YOU CAN TRUST IT (we test the radar against independent data, and we publish what did not work)

  • Where the optical map shows new buildings in 2015–2020, radar dates them to those years 46 times more often than on land that stayed open (95% interval 40–53). NISAR confirms buildings that Sentinel-1 dates to 2021–2024 22 times more often than open land (20–24).
  • After 2020, radar sees 1,839 ha of new or denser built-up area around Poznań, 393 ha inside the city.
  • Strong radar brightening is about 4 times as common on plots with a 2026 new-building permit from the Poznań city hall (16 of 766 cells, 8 decisions; block-bootstrap 95% interval about 1.7–7).
  • EGMS: where measured, typical ground motion is 0 mm/yr; 147 cells sink by 5 mm/yr or faster.
  • Not confirmed (shown as information, not warnings): radar dating of buildings on 2026 permit plots (interval 0.3–4.8); ALOS PALSAR 2007–2010 is not good enough for dating; a projection trained on radar alone failed an independent test and is not in the app.

All tests and numbers are reproducible from scripts in the repository.

BENEFITS

  • Home buyers get an independent, free check of the ground before the biggest purchase of their life.
  • Residents see what is being built around them and how fast green areas disappear.
  • City planners, banks and insurers get an open, testable land-risk overview from public satellite data.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

A "Check the ground" button next to every property listing, and the same method for any city in the world: NISAR covers the whole globe every 12 days, so as its time series grows, SARnik can move from "what was built" to "what is changing right now", including ground motion from NISAR itself.

TOOLS

Python (rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow, pystac-client, Microsoft Planetary Computer), JavaScript, Leaflet 1.9.4, MapLibre GL 4.7.1, Firebase Hosting, GitHub Actions with automated tests. Source code: https://github.com/MichallMaciek/NASA-SpaceWalkers

AI USE

We wrote the code and documentation with the help of AI coding assistants (Claude Code by Anthropic, Google Antigravity). The idea, the study area, the choice of data and the scientific tests are our own. Every number in the app comes from the listed satellite and official data, computed by our scripts and checked by automated tests; no data are AI-generated. No AI-generated images, video or audio are used: the demo is a plain screen recording of the app. AI use is also stated on the app's About page, and AI-assisted commits in the repository are marked "Co-Authored-By: Claude".

OPERA DIST-ALERT-S1 surface disturbance (NASA JPL) via Earthdata
ALOS PALSAR 2007-2010 via NASA ASF DAAC
MODIS Terra land surface temperature (MOD11) and vegetation (MOD13)
NASA POWER soil moisture (NASA Langley Research Center)
Landsat (NASA/USGS), used through GHSL and Hansen Global Forest Change
projectRefs: ISRO (Indian Space Research Organisation): NISAR co-builder
ESA/Copernicus Sentinel-1 RTC 2015-2026 (via Microsoft Planetary Computer)
Copernicus European Ground Motion Service (EGMS, InSAR 2016-2020)
ERA5 weather (Copernicus C3S) via Open-Meteo, CC BY 4.0
JAXA ALOS PALSAR and ALOS-2 PALSAR-2 L-band mosaics
Hansen Global Forest Change (University of Maryland)
GUGiK: ULDK cadastral parcels and Geoportal orthophoto (Polish Head Office of Geodesy and Cartography)
GEOPOZ Poznan: orthophoto 2025 and WUIA building decisions
GUS BDL (Statistics Poland, Local Data Bank)
OpenFreeMap vector base map (data: OpenStreetMap contributors)
acorn JavaScript parser (MIT, used in tests)
Claude / Claude Code by Anthropic (AI coding assistant)
